issues.issue: The preamble treats "Fund" and "Plan" as interchangeable labels for the same thing, whereas operative Sections 1.20 and 1.22 give "Plan" (the benefit rules) and "Trust Fund" (the assets) distinct meanings. A dispute over which body of terms governs could turn on that recital-versus-definition mismatch.

The recital says the Collective Bargaining Agreements "establish the Plan," but operative Section 1.20 defines the Plan as rules "from time to time adopted by the Board" and Section 4.2 vests amendment of the Plan in the Board. A party arguing the CBA fixes plan terms would rely on the recital against the operative text.

The recital limits the Trust to the "exclusive purpose of providing pension and retirement benefits," while operative Section 2.2 and Section 5.3 also authorise financing the operation and administration of the Trust and paying its expenses. The recital and the operative expense provisions point in different directions on what the corpus may be spent on.

The recital rests the amendment power on "Paragraph 18 of the Trust Agreement," a paragraph number that exists nowhere in the restated instrument, whose amendment provision is Section 10.1. That dangling cross-reference leaves the asserted authority unverifiable on the face of the document.

Section 1.1 lets the "Administrator" be the Board itself or a delegate, while Section 1.6 fixes the Board as the ERISA "administrator" and Section 7.1 assigns distinct duties to an Administrator. Which entity bears an Administrator duty in a given case is left uncertain across those provisions.

The definition names the "Publishers' Association of New York," whereas the preamble and the signature block identify the party as the Publishers' Association of New York City. The dropped word makes the defined party's identity turn on a scrivener's slip.

"Both the Chairman and Secretary of the Board" is ambiguous as to whether an Authorized Person means the two officers acting jointly or each of them individually. The rest of the definition, which lists single individuals in the alternative, does not resolve it.

"Internal Revenue Code of 1936" is a mechanical error; there is no such Code, and the instrument elsewhere invokes Sections 401(a), 501(a) and 4975, which are provisions of the 1986 Code. The mistake makes the defined term literally refer to a non-existent statute.

A writing counts as a "Collective Bargaining Agreement" only if it "is acceptable to the Board," a standard with no criteria and no procedure for acceptance. Whether a given participation agreement qualifies is therefore left to an unbounded judgment.

The definition incorporates the Collective Trust's own agreement by reference "to the extent not inconsistent with the terms of this Agreement," while simultaneously giving that trust's trustees "sole and exclusive authority" over transferred assets in tension with Section 5.7's diversification and prudence duty. Which document governs a transferred asset is left to be worked out.

Section 1.10 requires only "at least one Employer Trustee and one Union Trustee," while Section 5.6(b) requires two or more Trustees in equal numbers from each side. The two composition rules for the same body are stated differently.

The definition invokes "Corporate Trustee" "as that term is defined in Section 3.12," but Section 3.12 contains no definition — it only authorises the Board to appoint a bank or trust company as one. The cross-reference points to a definition that does not exist.

An Employer Trustee is defined solely as one "designated pursuant to Section 3.3(a)," which names two specific individuals, yet successors are designated under Section 3.9 by certificate of the Association. On the literal definition a Section 3.9 successor is not an Employer Trustee.

The definition requires Instructions to be "written communications signed by an Authorized Person," then expressly includes telex and similar transmissions that carry no signature and are validated only by a "reasonable degree of certainty" as to the sender. The signature requirement and the included examples cannot both be applied literally.

The definition makes it a condition of being an Investment Manager that the appointee "has acknowledged in writing to the Board" its fiduciary status, whereas Section 8.3 makes obtaining that acknowledgment optional ("The Board may require"). An appointee without a certificate is simultaneously an Investment Manager under Article 8 and not one under Section 1.18.

Section 1.20 defines "Plan" as the Board's benefit rules, but the Preamble uses "Plan" as an alternative name for the Fund itself. The same defined term carries two different referents in the instrument.

The definition is an enumerated list of eleven categories introduced by "including, but not limited to" and closed by catch-all (k), so the reach of the general words against the specific enumeration is open. Whether an instrument outside the list is a "Security" is left to ejusdem generis argument.

Section 1.22 sweeps in all property deposited in the trust account or held by a Custodian, while Section 5.5(w) directs that contributions collected for another plan be segregated and "shall not be deemed plan assets of the Fund." Whether segregated monies are Trust Fund assets depends on which provision controls.

"And any affiliates thereof" is undefined and sets no test for affiliation, so the set of labour organisations whose agreements bind the Fund has no stated boundary. Whether a particular local is within the "Union" cannot be answered from the text.

A Union Trustee is defined as one designated under Section 3.3(b), which names three individuals, but Section 3.8 provides that the Union Trustees "shall be the incumbent president, vice president and secretary-treasurer of the Union." If a named individual leaves office the two provisions identify different people as Union Trustees.

"Certain pension and related benefits" leaves the class of permissible "related" benefits undefined, and Section 4.1(a) compounds it by allowing whatever "related benefits as the Board may from time to time determine." The exclusive-purpose limit has no ascertainable boundary.

Section 2.3 provides that the Agreement "shall be deemed amended" automatically wherever it is inconsistent with the Code or ERISA, whereas Section 10.1 permits amendment only by unanimous vote of the Board subject to stated conditions. A self-executing amendment mechanism cannot be squared with the exclusive amendment procedure.

Section 2.4 makes participation depend on the employer being "acceptable to the Trustees," while Section 1.13 defines an Employer as any employer required to contribute under a Collective Bargaining Agreement with the Union, without any acceptance requirement. Whether an unaccepted signatory is bound to contribute turns on which provision governs.

The Employer is "deemed" to have "agreed to be bound unconditionally" to the Plan, the Trust and "all of the decisions of the Trustees," a deemed consent whose scope — including future amendments and future decisions — is left open. The word "unconditionally" would have to be construed against the limits the Employer actually accepted by signing a CBA.

Section 3.1 fixes an unequal board of two Employer and three Union Trustees, which sits awkwardly with Section 6.3's quorum of two from each side and with Section 10.1(c)'s premise of equal voting power, and it is flatly displaced by Amendment No. 4's two-and-two composition. Which composition governs at a given date is a live question on the face of the document.

The three named Union Trustees are fixed by name, while Section 3.8 provides that the Union Trustees "shall be the incumbent president, vice president and secretary-treasurer of the Union." The two provisions identify Union Trustees by different criteria and can diverge the moment an officer changes.

Section 3.1 states that "the appointment of Trustees shall be governed by the provisions of Section 3.4," but Section 3.4 prescribes no appointment mechanism at all — it only requires that copies of appointments be filed and acceptances signed. The referenced governing provision is empty of the substance it is said to supply.

Section 3.6 requires notice to "the Contributing Employer that designated him as a Trustee" and deems a Trustee resigned when "the Contributing Employer which designated him" ceases contributing, yet under Sections 3.1, 3.3, 3.7 and 3.9 Employer Trustees are designated by the Association and Union Trustees by the Union — no Contributing Employer designates anyone. The automatic-resignation trigger cannot be applied to any Trustee actually appointed under this instrument.

The section is headed "Removal of Union Trustees" but contains no removal power at all; it prescribes who the Union Trustees shall be and addresses only removal "by operation of law." Whether the Union may remove its Trustees, and by what means, is unanswerable from the provision that purports to govern it.

Section 3.8 makes the Union Trustees the incumbent president, vice president and secretary-treasurer ex officio, while Section 3.1 says they are "selected by the Union" and Section 3.3(b) names three individuals. The three provisions supply three different rules for who holds the office.

The sentence says the principal officer "shall designate a successor Union Trustee by filing... a certification," then adds "in which case a Successor Union Trustee shall be elected from the full-time officers of the Union." Designation by one officer and election from among the officers are two different mechanisms and the provision commands both.

Section 1.12 treats "Corporate Trustee" as a term "defined in Section 3.12," but 3.12(a) only confers a power of appointment and defines nothing. The definitional chain between the two provisions is broken.

The delegation closes with "such other duties and powers as the Board may deem advisable" after two specific grants, leaving the reach of the general words against the enumerated specifics open. Whether non-investment fiduciary functions can be handed to the Corporate Trustee turns on that catch-all.

Allowing the Corporate Trustee to hold the Fund "as sole trustee of a trust separate from the Fund created by this Trust Agreement" is hard to reconcile with Section 1.22, which defines the Trust Fund to include property held by a Custodian, and with Section 7.2's allocation of overall responsibility to the Board. Whether assets so held remain Trust Fund assets is left unresolved.

The clause releases the Trustees "forever" from "any responsibility or liability" for transferred assets, while Section 5.9 opens "Except as may otherwise be provided by ERISA" and Section 5.7 imposes a continuing prudence and diversification duty on the Board. The unqualified release cannot be squared with those provisions.

The limitation permits "no benefits other than pension, retirement, and such other related benefits as the Board may from time to time determine," so the general words at the end dissolve the very restriction the specifics create. What falls outside the enumerated categories is a matter the Board defines for itself.

Section 4.2 lets the Board amend the Plan "from time to time" or terminate it "at any time" without qualification, whereas Section 10.1 permits amendment only by unanimous Board vote subject to three express conditions and Section 10.2 forbids any amendment diverting the Fund. The unconditional grant and the conditioned grant cover the same act.

The three conditions (a), (b) and (c) are run together with the trailing fragment about Section 404 deductibility appearing out of sequence, so it cannot be told which condition attaches to which return period. As written the enumerated triggers and the enumerated deadlines do not line up.

Section 4.4 authorises the Board to return contributions to an Employer, while Section 10.3(b) states that "[u]nder no circumstances shall any portion of the corpus or income of the Trust Fund, directly or indirectly, revert or accrue to the benefit of any Employer" and Section 10.2 excepts only Section 10.3. The absolute no-reversion language does not carve out Section 4.4.

The anti-alienation rule is qualified by enumerated statutory exceptions (QDROs, Section 206(d)(2) assignments) followed by the open catch-all "or as may otherwise be provided in the Plan, ERISA or the Code," leaving the reach of the general words against the specifics undefined. Because the Board writes the Plan, the exception can be read to swallow the rule.

"All reasonable and necessary expenses" is followed by a seven-item list introduced by "including, but not limited to," so whether an unlisted charge is payable from the corpus turns on the reach of the general words. The specifics give no principle for the catch-all.

Section 5.3(c) lets the Board delegate "such of its administrative duties" as it deems advisable, while Section 5.13 limits delegation to "ministerial powers or duties" and Section 5.6(a) governs delegation of fiduciary responsibilities to Committees. The three provisions set different limits on the same delegation power.

Subsection (y) authorises the Board "[g]enerally, [to] perform all acts (whether or not expressly authorized herein)" it deems necessary and prudent, a catch-all standing against twenty-four enumerated specific powers. Whether the general words are confined to the kind of acts enumerated is exactly the ejusdem generis question.

The opening words empower the Board "in its sole and absolute discretion" free of state-law limits on trust investment, while Section 5.7 subjects every exercise of power under the Agreement to a prudent-person standard and a diversification requirement. Sole and absolute discretion and a prudence duty pull against each other over the same acts.

Section 5.6(a) permits delegation of "fiduciary responsibilities" to Committees "including but not limited to" benefit applications and delinquencies, while Section 5.13 confines the Board's delegation power to "ministerial powers or duties." The scope of what may be handed off differs between the two sections.

Section 5.6(b) requires each Committee to have an equal number of Employer and Union Trustees, whereas Section 1.10 requires only "at least one Employer Trustee and one Union Trustee." A committee valid under one definition may be invalid under the other.

Section 5.7 imposes a prudent-person standard of care on every exercise of power, while Section 5.9(b) states the Trustees "shall not be personally liable for any error of judgment or for any loss arising out of any act or omission." A duty that can never be breached in damages is difficult to reconcile with the stated standard.

The clause lets Trustees treat an employer's writing as "conclusive evidence" with "no duty to make any investigation or inquiry," while Section 5.7 requires the care and diligence of a prudent person familiar with such matters. Whether a Trustee may rely without inquiry in the face of red flags is unresolved between them.

Section 5.9(a) charges the Trust Fund with "first liens" indemnifying the Trustees against "any liabilities of any kind," while Section 5.9(d) indemnifies only good-faith conduct and excludes fraud, willful misconduct and gross negligence. The two subsections of the same section set incompatible indemnity boundaries.

The blanket exculpation for "any error of judgment or... any loss arising out of any act or omission" contradicts Section 5.9(d), which expressly withholds protection for a Trustee's own fraud, willful misconduct or gross negligence, and Section 5.7's prudence standard. Read literally, subsection (b) immunises the very conduct subsection (d) carves out.

The final exclusion reads "or except as may otherwise reimbursed by insurance," omitting the verb, so it is unclear whether insurance recovery bars indemnity or merely reduces it. The gap changes who bears a loss that insurance partly covers.

Section 5.9(d) limits indemnity to good-faith acts and excludes fraud, willful misconduct and gross negligence, while Section 5.9(b) exculpates Trustees for "any act or omission" without qualification. The two provisions cannot both govern the same claim.

Section 5.12(b) allows signature authority over Fund monies to be delegated to "any two Trustees" or even to a non-Trustee, while Section 6.4(a) requires all Board action to be by unanimous vote of the two units. Whether a two-Trustee withdrawal is Board action is left unaddressed.

Section 5.13 confines delegation to "ministerial powers or duties," but Section 5.6(a) authorises delegation of fiduciary responsibilities to Committees and Section 5.5(r) authorises delegation of Plan operation duties to other persons. The instrument states two inconsistent limits on the same power.

"Complete authority, in its sole and absolute discretion, to construe the terms of the Plan or this Agreement" with decisions "final and binding upon all parties affected thereby" leaves open who counts as a party affected and what review, if any, survives. The breadth of "final and binding" is precisely the sort of term parties read differently.

The Board's self-declared final authority to construe the Agreement sits against Section 6.6, which sends questions the Board cannot decide to an AAA arbitrator, and Section 9.10, which sends employer withdrawal-liability disputes to arbitration only. Whether the Board's construction binds an Employer in those forums is unresolved.

Officer terms run "until their successors are elected," yet no provision of Article 6 or elsewhere prescribes how or when officers are elected. The instrument supplies a term of office with no election mechanism to measure it against.

Special meetings may be called "by any four Trustees," but Section 3.1 provides for only five Trustees and Amendment No. 4's replacement Section 3.1 for only four. Under the amended composition the provision requires every Trustee to join in calling a meeting, which is no minority right at all.

A quorum of two Union and two Employer Trustees is workable under the original Section 3.1 (two and three), but Amendment No. 4 reduces the Board to two and two, so the quorum requirement becomes attendance by every Trustee. Whether a quorum can still be constituted after the amendment is a genuine question across the two provisions.

The subsection first requires "unanimous vote of the Trustees" and then "unanimous vote of the two units," which are different requirements — unanimity of individuals versus unanimity of two block votes. Section 6.4(b), which lets a unit vote be cast on a bare majority, shows the two formulations cannot both be literal.

A unit vote requires "the concurring vote of a majority of all" that unit's Trustees, which cannot be produced by a two-member unit that splits, yet Amendment No. 4's Section 3.1 fixes each unit at two Trustees. The voting rule assumes an odd-numbered unit the amended composition does not provide.

"Such proxies to be valid only at the meeting immediately succeeding its execution" is ambiguous as to whether the proxy is good at the next meeting of any kind or only at the meeting for which it was given. The singular "its" against the plural "proxies" adds to the uncertainty.

Section 6.4(d) provides that a deadlocked matter "shall then be resolved by arbitration," while Section 6.6(a) makes submission depend on a Trustee's request to the Chairman. Whether arbitration is automatic or must be invoked differs between the two provisions.

"Unless otherwise specifically agreed to by both parties" presupposes two parties, but a Section 6.6 arbitration arises from a deadlock among Trustees of a single board with no defined "parties." Whose agreement can move the hearing is not answerable from the text.

The opening sentence — "Where the Administrator is a Trust Fund, subject to the terms of this Agreement..." — has no predicate, so the provision never says what the Administrator is responsible for before listing "such responsibilities." The antecedent for the enumerated duties is missing.

Item (1) gives the Board "the right to amend, modify or terminate this Agreement at any time," whereas Section 10.1 permits amendment only by unanimous vote subject to three conditions and Section 10.3(a) also allows termination by joint resolution of the Union and the Association. The unconditional grant in 7.2 cannot be squared with Article 10's machinery.

"The Board shall meet periodically" fixes no interval and no benchmark, so whether the monitoring obligation has been performed cannot be measured from the text. The duty is mandatory in form but indeterminate in content.

Section 8.3 makes the fiduciary and Section 3(38) acknowledgment optional ("The Board may require"), while Section 1.18 makes an appointee an "Investment Manager" only if it "has acknowledged in writing to the Board" that status. The status of a manager appointed without a certificate differs under the two provisions.

The exception "except subsections (3) through (y)" cites a subsection "(3)" that does not exist in Section 5.5, whose subsections run (a) to (y). Which powers are withheld from the Investment Manager therefore cannot be determined from the words used.

Section 8.5 relieves the Board of responsibility for "any acts or omissions of any Investment Manager," while Section 8.2(c) requires it to meet periodically and monitor performance and Section 7.2(13) requires it to monitor and evaluate managers. A monitoring duty with a blanket disclaimer of responsibility for the monitored party is internally awkward.

"Shall be the sole responsibility of the Board" is ambiguous between meaning that only the Board decides an Investment Manager's authority and meaning that the Board alone bears liability for it. The two readings have opposite consequences for a loss caused by a manager.

If "sole responsibility" imports liability, Section 8.7 contradicts Section 8.5, which states that neither the Board nor the Administrator "shall be responsible or liable for any acts or omissions of any Investment Manager." The two adjacent sections would then allocate the same risk in opposite directions.

Section 9.1 provides that contribution rates are "at all times" governed by the Collective Bargaining Agreements and that nothing in the Trust Agreement changes their terms, yet Sections 9.4(b), 9.5(b) and 9.7 impose interest, twenty-percent liquidated damages and fee liability that no CBA need contain. Whether an Employer owes those Trust-Agreement charges is a direct clash between the two.

The paragraph says collection costs "shall be paid from the Fund" and then introduces the enforcement power with "Notwithstanding the preceding sentence," although the enforcement power does not contradict who bears collection costs. The misplaced connector obscures whether the Fund or the delinquent Employer bears those costs.

Section 9.4(a) assesses interest "at a rate calculated in accordance with Section 9.5," but Section 9.5 sets no calculation method — it states a flat 18 percent (and, as amended, whatever rate "the Trustees deem appropriate"). The cross-reference points to a method that does not exist.

"Liquidated damage penalty" combines two mutually exclusive characterisations, and whether the greater-of-interest-or-twenty-percent sum is compensatory or penal is what its enforceability turns on. The provision labels the same amount both ways.

Sections 9.4(a) and 9.7(b)-(c) refer to interest "calculated in accordance with the method set forth in Section 9.5," but 9.5(b) supplies only a flat rate buried in a list of recoverable expenses, and Amendment No. 2 replaces it with an open discretion. The rate actually payable depends on reconciling those provisions.

The parenthetical "(hereinafter collectively referred to as 'unpaid contributions')" follows a list of agreements and rules, not a sum of money, so the defined term has no grammatical antecedent in amounts owed. Section 9.7 then builds its whole damages formula on that mis-anchored definition.

Subsections (b) and (c) compute interest "in accordance with the method set forth in Section 9.5," but Section 9.5 states a bare rate rather than a method, and Amendment No. 2 replaces that rate with whatever the Trustees deem appropriate. The award formula depends on a referenced method the instrument never sets out.

"All records deemed necessary by such persons" makes the auditors the sole judges of the scope of an Employer's production obligation, with no stated limit. The boundary of what must be handed over cannot be fixed from the words.

"Any and all claims by third parties (including Employers) against the Trust Fund concerning the assessment... of withdrawal liability" does not say whether a dispute the Fund itself initiates, or a challenge to the methodology rather than the assessment, falls inside the arbitration-only channel. The scope of "claims against the Trust Fund" is exactly what two sides would read differently.

The section says such disputes "shall not become the subject of litigation in the courts" and shall be determined "only by arbitration," yet its final sentence preserves the Fund's right to sue in State or Federal court under Section 4221(b)(1), and Sections 9.5(a) and 9.6 authorise court enforcement generally. Whether the court door is shut depends on reconciling those provisions.

Section 10.1 allows amendment only by unanimous Board vote and subject to conditions (a)-(c), while Section 7.2(1)-(2) states the Board's right to "amend, modify or terminate this Agreement at any time" and Section 4.2 gives the same unconditioned power over the Plan. The instrument grants the amendment power twice on different terms.

Section 10.2 forbids any amendment returning Fund assets to Contributing Employers "except as otherwise provided in Section 10.3," but Section 10.3(b) states that "[u]nder no circumstances" shall any corpus revert to an Employer — so the referenced exception contains no exception. Section 4.4, which does permit returns, is not cross-referenced at all.

Termination route (2), "a joint resolution adopted by the Union and the Association," gives non-Board parties power to end the Trust, whereas Section 7.2(1) and Section 10.1 vest the right to terminate the Agreement in the Board acting unanimously. Who may pull the plug differs between Article 7 and Article 10.

Distribution of "any remaining surplus in a manner consistent, in their opinion, with this Agreement, the Plan, ERISA, the Code and any other applicable law" supplies no distributive rule at all, only the Trustees' opinion. Who receives the surplus and in what shares is left unstated.

The absolute statement that "[u]nder no circumstances" shall corpus or income revert to any Employer cannot be squared with Section 4.4, which authorises returning mistaken, disqualified or non-deductible contributions to the Employer. The two provisions govern the same money in opposite directions.

"Such commercially acceptable valuation method or methods determined by the Board" identifies no method and no external benchmark, leaving fair market value to be fixed by the valuer itself. For illiquid assets the phrase gives no ascertainable standard.

"The New York City metropolitan area" has no defined boundary and could include counties in New Jersey and Connecticut, yet the clause also deems the Board "located at that address" for legal purposes. Where the Board is deemed located, and thus what venue follows, turns on an undefined geographic term.

Section 12.6 makes conclusive "every certificate or other instrument executed by the Chairman" alone, while Section 5.15 authorises execution on the Board's behalf only by the Chairman and Secretary together, or by a resolution-authorised pair of one Union and one Employer Trustee. A third party's protection and the Board's actual signing rule do not match.

Section 12.7 imports every definition from the Plan into this Agreement, while Article 1 defines the same core terms — "Plan," "Covered Employee," "Employer" — for the Agreement itself, and the Board may rewrite the Plan unilaterally under Section 4.2. Which definition governs where the two documents differ is unresolved.

Notice is "deemed duly given... when deposited by first-class mail," but the closing sentence deems it given "as of the date on which it is" — the sentence stops without stating the date. The provision supplies two deeming rules and completes only one.

The clause denies any right to benefits "unless and until the Board determines that he fulfills all the requirements" of the Plan, while Section 4.2 and Section 5.2 make the written Plan the source of entitlement and require the Board to pay the benefits provided for there. Whether entitlement arises from the Plan terms or only from a Board determination is a real difference.

The trailing qualifier "except as set forth in the Plan" can attach either to the denial of any interest in Fund assets or also to the denial of any right to continued employment, which would be an absurd reading. Which limb it modifies changes the provision's effect.

"18 percent per annum or such other interest rate that the Trustees deem appropriate given the circumstance" supplies no ceiling, no floor and no criteria, so the rate is whatever the creditor later decides. The added words make the previously fixed rate indeterminate.

Sections 9.4(a), 9.7(b) and 9.7(c) all compute amounts "in accordance with the method set forth in Section 9.5," but as amended Section 9.5(b) no longer sets any method — only a discretion. The amendment leaves those cross-references pointing at nothing determinate.

"The appointment of Trustees shall be selected by the provisions of Section 3.4" is ungrammatical — appointments are governed, not selected — and Section 3.4 in any event prescribes no appointment procedure. The sentence states a governing rule that neither reads nor exists.

Reducing the Board to two Employer and two Union Trustees makes Section 6.2(b)'s "any four Trustees" and Section 6.3's quorum of two from each side require the whole Board, and leaves Section 6.4(b)'s "majority of all" the Trustees in a unit unachievable on a two-member split. The amended composition cannot be worked with Article 6 as drafted.

The two Union Trustees are fixed by name, while amended Section 3.8 provides that the Union Trustees "shall be the incumbent president and vice president/secretary treasurer of the Union." If a named individual ceases to hold that office the two provisions identify different Trustees.

The section is headed "Removal of Union Trustees" but confers no power of removal; it prescribes who holds the office and deals only with removal "by operation of law." How the Union may in fact remove a Trustee is unanswerable from the provision that purports to govern removal.

Amended Section 3.8 makes the Union Trustees ex officio the incumbent president and vice president/secretary-treasurer, while amended Section 3.3(b) names two specific individuals and Section 3.10 has a successor "designate[d]" by the principal officer yet also "elected from the full-time officers." The three provisions give three different routes to the same office.
